cards.q: In smooth muscle, which protein does calcium bind to in order to start contraction?
cards.a: Calmodulin.
options: Calmodulin
Tropomyosin
Actin
Troponin C
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle has no troponin, so the Ca2+ receptor is calmodulin, a soluble protein floating in the cytosol rather than sitting on the thin filament. Four Ca2+ bind calmodulin, and that complex is what switches on the next enzyme in the pathway. Troponin C is the Ca2+ receptor in skeletal and cardiac muscle, which is the single most useful contrast to carry out of this chapter. Tropomyosin blocks myosin binding sites in striated muscle but does not bind the activating Ca2+, and actin is the thin filament itself.

cards.q: What does the Ca2+ calmodulin complex activate in smooth muscle?
cards.a: Myosin light chain kinase.
options: Phospholipase C
Myosin light chain phosphatase
Protein kinase A
Myosin light chain kinase
cards.explanation: Ca2+ calmodulin binds and activates myosin light chain kinase, the enzyme that turns a Ca2+ signal into a working cross bridge. Myosin light chain phosphatase does the opposite job and is not Ca2+ activated, so it runs steadily in the background and drives relaxation when the kinase quiets down. Protein kinase A is activated by cAMP, not by Ca2+ calmodulin, and in smooth muscle it tends to promote relaxation. Phospholipase C sits upstream: it makes IP3 that raises Ca2+ in the first place.

cards.q: Once activated, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates what?
cards.a: The regulatory light chain on the myosin head.
options: The troponin I subunit on the thin filament
A serine on the tropomyosin strand
The regulatory light chain on the myosin head
The actin monomer at the myosin binding site
cards.explanation: The target is a small regulatory light chain sitting on the neck of the myosin head, and phosphorylating it lets that head bind actin and cycle. Because the switch is on myosin, smooth muscle regulation is called thick filament regulation, in contrast to the thin filament regulation of striated muscle. Troponin I is not present in smooth muscle at all. Tropomyosin is present but is not the phosphorylation target, and actin itself is never phosphorylated to turn contraction on.

cards.q: Where does most of the Ca2+ that activates smooth muscle contraction come from?
cards.a: The extracellular fluid, entering through Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane.
options: Ca2+ pried off troponin when the cell depolarizes
The extracellular fluid, through plasma membrane Ca2+ channels
The sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is very extensive in this tissue
Mitochondrial stores dumped at the start of contraction
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle has only a sparse sarcoplasmic reticulum, so it leans on Ca2+ entering from outside through voltage gated and ligand gated channels, with a smaller contribution released from the SR. That dependence is why smooth muscle tone collapses quickly in a low Ca2+ bath and why Ca2+ channel blockers relax blood vessels. The SR answer describes skeletal muscle, where the store is large and self sufficient. Mitochondria buffer Ca2+ rather than supply it, and there is no troponin in smooth muscle to hold Ca2+.

cards.q: Which enzyme dephosphorylates the myosin light chain and allows smooth muscle to relax?
cards.a: Myosin light chain phosphatase.
options: Phospholipase C
Myosin light chain phosphatase
Adenylyl cyclase
Myosin light chain kinase
cards.explanation: Relaxation is not simply the absence of Ca2+; a phosphatase has to strip the phosphate off the myosin light chain before the head stops cycling. Myosin light chain kinase adds that phosphate, so it is the on switch, not the off switch. Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, which promotes relaxation indirectly by reducing kinase activity, but it does not touch the light chain. Phospholipase C acts upstream to raise Ca2+, which pushes the cell toward contraction rather than relaxation.

cards.q: Which intracellular messenger releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of smooth muscle?
cards.a: IP3.
options: IP3
cGMP
Diacylglycerol
cAMP
cards.explanation: IP3 is made when a Gq coupled receptor activates phospholipase C, and it opens IP3 receptor channels on the SR to let stored Ca2+ into the cytosol. cAMP and cGMP both favor relaxation in smooth muscle rather than Ca2+ release; cGMP is the messenger nitric oxide works through. Diacylglycerol is the other product of phospholipase C, but it stays in the membrane and activates protein kinase C instead of releasing Ca2+.

cards.q: What is the latch state in smooth muscle?
cards.a: Sustained tension held by cross bridges that cycle very slowly and use little ATP.
options: The rigor condition that appears when cellular ATP is exhausted
A burst of extra force produced as Ca2+ first enters the cell
A refractory period after contraction when the cell cannot be restimulated
Sustained tension held by slowly cycling cross bridges at low ATP cost
cards.explanation: In the latch state, dephosphorylated myosin heads stay attached to actin and detach only very slowly, so tension holds while ATP use per second drops. This is the reason a sphincter or an arteriole can maintain tone for hours without exhausting the cell. It is not a refractory period, since smooth muscle can be restimulated during it. Rigor is a pathological state from lack of ATP, and unlike latch it cannot be reversed by the cell.

cards.q: How does the ATPase activity of smooth muscle myosin compare with that of skeletal muscle myosin?
cards.a: It is far slower, which is why shortening velocity is low.
options: About the same, with speed set only by Ca2+ removal
Somewhat faster, offset by having fewer cross bridges
Far slower, which is why shortening velocity is low
Far faster, but limited by the small sarcoplasmic reticulum
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle myosin splits ATP roughly ten to several hundred times more slowly than skeletal myosin, so each cross bridge cycle takes longer and the muscle shortens slowly. That same slow cycling is what makes smooth muscle economical, because a head spends most of its cycle attached and bearing load. Slow Ca2+ removal does prolong relaxation, but it is not the reason shortening itself is slow. Nothing about smooth muscle myosin is faster than skeletal myosin.

cards.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane of an arteriole. What happens to myosin light chain kinase activity and to vessel tone?
cards.a: Both fall, so the vessel dilates.
options: MLCK activity is unchanged because its Ca2+ comes from the SR
MLCK activity falls but tone stays the same
MLCK activity falls and the vessel dilates
MLCK activity rises and the vessel constricts
cards.explanation: Blocking the channel cuts Ca2+ entry, less Ca2+ calmodulin forms, MLCK activity drops, and with the phosphatase still working the light chains are dephosphorylated and the vessel dilates. Tone cannot stay the same, because in smooth muscle tension tracks the fraction of phosphorylated light chains. The SR answer would be closer to the truth in skeletal muscle, where the store supplies nearly all the activator Ca2+ and channel blockers barely change force. Nothing in this pathway increases kinase activity.

cards.q: A signaling pathway inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase while cytosolic Ca2+ stays constant. What happens to tension?
cards.a: Tension rises at that same Ca2+ level.
options: Tension briefly rises and then returns to baseline
Tension rises at that same Ca2+ level
Tension falls because the kinase is inhibited as well
Tension is unchanged because Ca2+ alone sets tension
cards.explanation: Tension follows the balance between the kinase adding phosphate and the phosphatase removing it, so slowing the phosphatase lets phosphorylated myosin accumulate even with no extra Ca2+. Physiologists call this Ca2+ sensitization, and it is how several vasoconstrictors work. The Ca2+ only answer is the common misreading: Ca2+ sets kinase activity, not tension directly. Nothing here touches the kinase, and the shift persists as long as the phosphatase is inhibited.

cards.q: A smooth muscle strip and a skeletal muscle fiber are moved into a Ca2+ free bath and stimulated repeatedly. Which one fails first, and why?
cards.a: The smooth muscle, because its activator Ca2+ comes from outside the cell.
options: The smooth muscle, because its activator Ca2+ comes from outside the cell
Both fail at about the same time, since both depend on Ca2+ entry
Neither fails, since both release their Ca2+ from the internal stores
The skeletal fiber, because it has no internal store of Ca2+ to draw on
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle depends on Ca2+ crossing the plasma membrane, so removing extracellular Ca2+ takes away most of its trigger within seconds to minutes. Skeletal muscle keeps twitching because the voltage sensor in the T tubule opens the SR release channel mechanically, with no Ca2+ influx required. Saying both fail together ignores that difference in Ca2+ source. Skeletal muscle does store Ca2+, in a large and well loaded sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Why does smooth muscle take much longer to reach peak tension than skeletal muscle after cytosolic Ca2+ rises?
cards.a: A kinase must phosphorylate myosin before cross bridges can cycle, and those bridges cycle slowly.
options: The action potential in smooth muscle is much longer than the twitch
Ca2+ must diffuse the length of a long T tubule network first
Troponin in smooth muscle binds Ca2+ more slowly than elsewhere
An enzyme must phosphorylate myosin before cross bridges can cycle
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle goes almost directly from Ca2+ binding troponin to cross bridge cycling, while smooth muscle inserts an enzymatic step: Ca2+ calmodulin must activate MLCK and MLCK must phosphorylate each myosin head. Add the slow myosin ATPase and peak tension can take a second or more instead of tens of milliseconds. Smooth muscle has no T tubules, using surface caveolae instead, and it has no troponin at all. The action potential length is not what sets the delay here.

cards.q: A vascular smooth muscle cell holds a steady contraction for an hour. Compared with the first few seconds, what happens to ATP consumption per unit of tension?
cards.a: It falls sharply as cross bridges settle into the latch state.
options: It stays constant, since tension and ATP use are proportional
It falls only because tension itself is fading
It rises steadily as more cross bridges are recruited
It falls sharply as cross bridges settle into the latch state
cards.explanation: Once tension is established, many heads are dephosphorylated while still attached, and they detach so slowly that ATP splitting per second drops far below what the same tension costs in skeletal muscle. Tension is maintained, so the last option has the cause backwards. ATP use and tension are proportional only if cycling rate is fixed, and the whole point of latch is that the cycling rate changes. Smooth muscle also has no motor units to recruit.

cards.q: A drug prevents Ca2+ from binding calmodulin. A smooth muscle cell is then stimulated and cytosolic Ca2+ rises normally. What tension develops?
cards.a: Little or none, because MLCK is never activated.
options: Normal tension, since Ca2+ itself activates the myosin head
Reduced tension, because Ca2+ binds troponin more slowly
Little or none, because MLCK is never activated
Increased tension, because free Ca2+ stays elevated longer
cards.explanation: Ca2+ has no direct effect on smooth muscle myosin; it works only through calmodulin, which activates MLCK, which phosphorylates the light chain. Break the calmodulin step and a normal Ca2+ signal produces nothing. Troponin is not in this tissue, so a slowed troponin response cannot be the answer. Higher free Ca2+ does not help either, because with calmodulin blocked there is no route from Ca2+ to a cycling cross bridge.

cards.q: Norepinephrine binds an alpha1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle and the cell contracts without firing a full action potential. Which pathway explains this?
cards.a: Gq activates phospholipase C, and IP3 releases Ca2+ from the SR.
options: Gs raises cAMP, which activates protein kinase A
Gq activates phospholipase C, and IP3 releases SR Ca2+
Nitric oxide raises cGMP, which activates protein kinase G
The receptor opens voltage gated Na+ channels directly
cards.explanation: Alpha1 receptors couple to Gq, so phospholipase C makes IP3, IP3 empties SR Ca2+ into the cytosol, and tension develops with no change in membrane potential. Physiologists call this pharmacomechanical coupling, and it is why smooth muscle can grade tone without spikes. The Gs and cAMP route is what beta2 receptors use, and in smooth muscle it favors relaxation. The cGMP route is the nitric oxide relaxation pathway. Receptors do not gate voltage dependent Na+ channels directly.

cards.q: In an artery preparation, agonist A doubles cytosolic Ca2+ and doubles tension. Agonist B doubles tension with no measurable change in Ca2+. What best explains agonist B?
cards.a: It inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase, so phosphorylated myosin builds up.
options: It inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase, so phosphorylated myosin builds up
It binds troponin C directly and bypasses the calmodulin pathway
It speeds the uptake of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during contraction
It opens more L-type Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane than A does
cards.explanation: Tension reflects the fraction of myosin light chains carrying a phosphate, and that fraction depends on kinase activity and phosphatase activity together. If tension doubles while Ca2+ is flat, the kinase side is unchanged, so the phosphatase side must have slowed. Opening more Ca2+ channels would have shown up as a Ca2+ rise, which is exactly what was not seen. There is no troponin in smooth muscle to bind. Faster SR uptake would lower Ca2+ and reduce tension, not raise it.

cards.q: A smooth muscle strip is stimulated and holds steady tension for twenty minutes. During that time cytosolic Ca2+ falls back toward baseline and the fraction of phosphorylated myosin light chains falls, yet tension barely changes. What accounts for the maintained tension?
cards.a: Dephosphorylated cross bridges stay attached and detach very slowly.
options: Dephosphorylated cross bridges remain attached and detach very slowly
Troponin continues to hold the thin filament in its activated position
The muscle has entered rigor because ATP has been depleted
A second wave of Ca2+ entry keeps the kinase fully active
cards.explanation: This is the latch state: heads that were phosphorylated earlier stay bound to actin after losing their phosphate, and because their detachment rate is very low the tension they carry persists. That is the mechanical basis of the economy of smooth muscle tone. A second Ca2+ wave is ruled out by the measurement, since Ca2+ was falling. Troponin is absent from smooth muscle. Rigor would be irreversible and would follow ATP depletion, which does not happen during ordinary sustained tone.

cards.q: A toxin selectively blocks IP3 receptors on the smooth muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. The tissue is then tested with a Gq coupled agonist and, separately, with a high K+ solution that depolarizes the membrane. What is the expected result?
cards.a: The response to the agonist is much reduced, while the response to high K+ is largely preserved.
options: The high K+ response is abolished while the agonist response stays normal
Both responses are normal, since IP3 acts only during relaxation
Both responses are abolished, since all of the activator Ca2+ is SR derived
The agonist response is much reduced, while the high K+ response is preserved
cards.explanation: The Gq agonist works largely by making IP3 and emptying the SR, so blocking IP3 receptors takes most of that route away. High K+ depolarizes the membrane and opens voltage gated Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane, a path that does not require IP3 at all, so that response survives. The first option would be right in skeletal muscle, where essentially all activator Ca2+ is SR derived. IP3 raises Ca2+ and promotes contraction, so it is not a relaxation signal.

cards.q: An internal anal sphincter and a skeletal muscle are each asked to hold the same tension for ten minutes. How does ATP use compare, and why?
cards.a: The smooth muscle uses far less ATP, because its cross bridges cycle slowly and stay attached.
options: The two use similar ATP, since tension and ATP cost are fixed together
The skeletal muscle uses less, because motor units can be rotated
The smooth muscle uses far less, because its cross bridges cycle slowly
The smooth muscle uses more, because it must keep MLCK active throughout
cards.explanation: Each ATP is spent on one cross bridge cycle, so the cost of holding tension depends on how often bridges detach and reattach, not on tension alone. Smooth muscle myosin cycles slowly and latch bridges hold on longer still, so the same force costs a fraction of the ATP. Rotating motor units spreads fatigue in skeletal muscle but does not lower the total ATP needed for a given tension. Keeping some MLCK activity is cheap compared with the cost of fast cycling cross bridges.

cards.q: Smooth muscle joined by many gap junctions contracts as one coordinated sheet. Which type is built this way, and where is it found?
cards.a: Single unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine.
options: Multi unit smooth muscle, as in the iris of the eye
Single unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine
Multi unit smooth muscle, as in the wall of the intestine
Single unit smooth muscle, as in the iris of the eye
cards.explanation: Single unit, also called visceral, smooth muscle is electrically coupled, so current spreads cell to cell through gap junctions and the layer behaves as a functional syncytium. The gut, ureter, uterus, and small blood vessels are built this way because a coordinated squeeze is the point. The iris is the standard example of the opposite arrangement, multi unit muscle, whose fibers are largely uncoupled. Pairing multi unit with the intestine or single unit with the iris swaps the two designs and their jobs.

cards.q: In the iris and the arrector pili muscles, fibers are largely uncoupled and each has its own autonomic ending. What does that arrangement make possible?
cards.a: Precise graded control of small numbers of fibers at a time.
options: Coordinated contraction of the whole sheet from one stimulus
Precise graded control of small numbers of fibers at a time
Spontaneous rhythmic contraction with no nerve input at all
Much faster conduction of excitation across the tissue
cards.explanation: Because the fibers are not electrically tied together, the nervous system can activate a few at a time and grade the response finely, which is what setting pupil size or lens shape demands. Contraction of the whole sheet from a single stimulus is the single unit design, and it depends on gap junctions this tissue mostly lacks. Spontaneous rhythm also comes from coupled pacemaker activity, so multi unit muscle is largely quiet without its nerves. Losing coupling slows the spread of excitation rather than speeding it.

cards.q: What are slow waves in single unit smooth muscle?
cards.a: Spontaneous rhythmic swings in membrane potential generated by pacemaker cells.
options: Spontaneous rhythmic swings in membrane potential from pacemaker cells
Long action potentials carried by a slow inward Ca2+ plateau current
Slowly spreading waves of Ca2+ released from the internal stores
Sustained depolarizations produced by continuous stretch of the wall
cards.explanation: Slow waves are subthreshold oscillations of the resting potential, set up by pacemaker cells such as the interstitial cells of Cajal and spread through gap junctions. When a wave crests above threshold it triggers a burst of spikes and a contraction, which is why gut motility has an underlying rhythm. A plateau bearing action potential describes cardiac muscle and some smooth muscle spikes, but it is not the pacemaker rhythm itself. Ca2+ waves are intracellular events, and stretch produces depolarization but not the intrinsic rhythm.

cards.q: How does an autonomic axon deliver its transmitter to smooth muscle?
cards.a: From varicosities along the axon that release transmitter into the surrounding space.
options: By direct current flow through gap junctions with the axon
Through capillaries after the transmitter enters the blood
Through a single tightly organized motor end plate per fiber
From varicosities along the axon into the surrounding space
cards.explanation: Autonomic axons run past smooth muscle cells and release transmitter from swellings called varicosities into a diffuse junction, so one axon can influence many cells and the transmitter reaches receptors across a wider gap. That diffuse arrangement is part of why smooth muscle responses are slower and more graded than a skeletal twitch. The tight motor end plate belongs to skeletal muscle. Neurons do not couple to smooth muscle electrically, and local transmitter is not delivered by way of the bloodstream, which is how hormones act.

cards.q: What is the myogenic response of smooth muscle?
cards.a: Contraction of the muscle in response to being stretched.
options: Loss of tone when the muscle is held at a fixed length
Relaxation of the muscle when it is stretched
Contraction of the muscle in response to being stretched
Contraction triggered by sympathetic nerve traffic
cards.explanation: Stretch opens mechanically sensitive channels, the cell depolarizes, voltage gated Ca2+ channels open, and the muscle contracts. In an arteriole this is the basis of autoregulation, since a rise in pressure meets a rise in resistance. Relaxation to stretch is the opposite of what is observed and would let a vessel balloon. Sympathetic constriction is a neural stimulus, not the myogenic one, and the myogenic response is defined by a change in length, not by holding one.

cards.q: Which set of local changes in an actively metabolizing tissue relaxes nearby arteriolar smooth muscle?
cards.a: Falling O2 with rising CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine.
options: Rising O2 with rising H+ and falling K+
Rising O2 with falling CO2 and falling adenosine
Falling O2 with rising CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine
Falling K+ with rising pH and rising O2
cards.explanation: Working tissue consumes O2 and produces CO2, H+, K+, and adenosine, and each of those changes relaxes the arteriolar smooth muscle upstream, so blood flow rises to meet demand. This is active hyperemia, and it is local: no nerve or hormone is required. The options built around rising O2 describe a tissue that is less active, which would allow tone to increase instead. Rising pH with falling K+ also points away from active metabolism.

cards.q: Which signal released by vascular endothelium relaxes the smooth muscle underneath it?
cards.a: Nitric oxide.
options: Angiotensin II
Nitric oxide
Thromboxane A2
Endothelin
cards.explanation: Nitric oxide diffuses from endothelium into the smooth muscle, raises cGMP, activates protein kinase G, and lowers cytosolic Ca2+ while promoting dephosphorylation of the myosin light chain, so the vessel dilates. Endothelin also comes from endothelium but is one of the strongest constrictors known. Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor rather than a local endothelial one. Thromboxane A2 comes mainly from platelets and constricts as well.

cards.q: What is meant by smooth muscle tone?
cards.a: A steady partial contraction maintained at rest.
options: A steady partial contraction maintained at rest
The maximum tension the muscle can generate
The passive stiffness of the connective tissue in the wall
The rate at which the muscle can be stretched
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle sits partly contracted most of the time, so a stimulus can raise tone or lower it from that baseline, giving a two way control range. Arterioles rely on this: without resting tone there would be no way to dilate. Maximum tension is a separate measurement made under full activation. Passive stiffness comes from elastin and collagen and persists in dead tissue, while tone requires living, Ca2+ handling muscle. Rate of stretch is a property of the load, not a state of the muscle.

cards.q: A drug uncouples the gap junctions in the wall of the small intestine. What happens to peristalsis?
cards.a: Coordinated waves are lost and contraction becomes patchy.
options: Nothing changes, since each fiber is separately innervated
The muscle becomes unable to contract at all
Contractions become stronger and better synchronized
Coordinated waves are lost and contraction becomes patchy
cards.explanation: Intestinal smooth muscle is single unit, so a pacemaker depolarization has to travel cell to cell through gap junctions to make a whole segment contract in sequence. Cut those connections and individual cells still contract, but not together, so propulsion fails. Separate innervation of every fiber describes multi unit muscle, not the gut. The cells retain their contractile machinery, so a complete loss of contraction is too strong a prediction.

cards.q: The ciliary muscle adjusts lens shape in small graded steps under autonomic control. Which classification does this behavior indicate?
cards.a: Multi unit smooth muscle.
options: Single unit smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Skeletal muscle under voluntary control
Multi unit smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Fine grading requires that the nervous system be able to activate some fibers and not others, which is only possible when the fibers are not electrically coupled. That uncoupled, individually innervated design is the definition of multi unit smooth muscle. Single unit muscle would move as one sheet and could not focus a lens smoothly. Cardiac muscle contracts as a whole by design, and the ciliary muscle is not under voluntary control, which rules out skeletal muscle.

cards.q: As the bladder fills, the smooth muscle in its wall is stretched. What is the immediate effect on membrane potential and on contraction?
cards.a: The membrane depolarizes and the muscle contracts.
options: The membrane potential is unchanged but Ca2+ still rises
The membrane depolarizes while contraction is suppressed
The membrane depolarizes and the muscle contracts
The membrane hyperpolarizes and the muscle relaxes
cards.explanation: Stretch opens mechanically gated cation channels, the cell depolarizes toward threshold, voltage gated Ca2+ channels open, and tension develops. Hyperpolarization would move the cell away from threshold and is the response to relaxing signals such as nitric oxide. Ca2+ can rise without a potential change when a Gq agonist acts, but stretch works through the membrane. Depolarization with suppressed contraction does not occur, because in smooth muscle depolarization is a route to Ca2+ entry.

cards.q: Perfusion pressure to an arteriole rises abruptly while tissue metabolism stays constant. What does the myogenic response predict for vessel radius and for flow?
cards.a: The vessel constricts, so flow rises much less than pressure did.
options: The vessel dilates, so flow rises in proportion to pressure
The vessel constricts, so flow rises much less than pressure did
The vessel is unchanged, so flow rises in proportion to pressure
The vessel constricts so hard that flow falls below baseline
cards.explanation: Higher pressure stretches the wall, the muscle depolarizes and contracts, and the smaller radius raises resistance, which blunts the rise in flow. That is autoregulation, and it protects downstream capillaries from a pressure surge. A dilating vessel would amplify the flow change rather than buffer it. An unchanged vessel would let flow track pressure directly. Autoregulation blunts the change, it does not overshoot into ischemia.

cards.q: A skeletal muscle goes from rest to heavy exercise and its metabolic rate rises sharply. What happens to the arterioles feeding it, and by what mechanism?
cards.a: They dilate, because local metabolites accumulate and relax the smooth muscle.
options: They dilate, because local metabolites accumulate and relax the muscle
They dilate, because circulating epinephrine reaches them first
They are unchanged, because flow is set entirely by blood pressure
They constrict, because sympathetic tone rises during exercise
cards.explanation: Adenosine, K+, CO2, and H+ build up faster than they are washed out, and each relaxes the arteriolar smooth muscle, so resistance falls and flow rises to match demand. This local control happens even in a denervated muscle, which is the classic evidence for it. Sympathetic tone does rise in exercise, but in working muscle the local metabolic signal overrides it. Epinephrine contributes at beta2 receptors, but the local metabolite effect is the dominant and faster mechanism, and flow is not set by pressure alone since resistance can change.

cards.q: Mast cells release histamine into an injured patch of skin. What is the effect on the local arteriolar smooth muscle and on the appearance of the skin?
cards.a: The muscle relaxes, so the arterioles dilate and the skin reddens.
options: The muscle relaxes, so the arterioles dilate and the skin reddens
The muscle is unaffected, since histamine acts only on capillaries
The muscle relaxes but skin color is unchanged, since flow is fixed
The muscle contracts, so the arterioles narrow and the skin pales
cards.explanation: Histamine is a local chemical signal that relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, and the resulting rise in local blood flow produces the redness and warmth of an inflamed area. Pallor would follow a constrictor such as norepinephrine acting on alpha1 receptors. Histamine also acts on venules to increase permeability and cause swelling, but it clearly acts on arteriolar muscle as well. Since resistance falls, flow is not fixed and the color change follows.

cards.q: In one artery ring the endothelium has been rubbed away; in a matching ring it is intact. Acetylcholine is added to both. The intact ring relaxes and the denuded ring constricts slightly. What explains the difference?
cards.a: Acetylcholine normally causes endothelium to release nitric oxide, and without endothelium it acts directly on the muscle.
options: Acetylcholine is broken down much faster when the endothelium is missing
The denuded ring lost its gap junctions, so the relaxation cannot spread through the wall
Rubbing the vessel damaged the underlying smooth muscle so it cannot relax
Acetylcholine releases nitric oxide from endothelium; without it, it acts on the muscle
cards.explanation: Acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors on endothelial cells, which raise nitric oxide, and nitric oxide raises cGMP in the smooth muscle and relaxes it. Strip the endothelium and acetylcholine reaches muscarinic receptors on the muscle itself, which raise Ca2+ and produce mild constriction. Mechanical damage to the muscle would abolish contraction as well as relaxation, and the denuded ring still contracts. Faster breakdown would produce no response rather than an opposite one, and gap junction loss would not reverse the sign of the response.

cards.q: Near the end of pregnancy, hormonal changes increase the number of gap junctions between uterine smooth muscle cells. Predict how the uterus behaves during labor and why.
cards.a: Excitation spreads farther, so contractions become coordinated and forceful.
options: The muscle loses its stretch sensitivity as coupling increases
Each cell becomes independently innervated, allowing graded contractions
Excitation spreads farther, so contractions become coordinated and forceful
Contractions weaken, because current leaks away from each cell
cards.explanation: More gap junctions mean stronger electrical coupling, so a depolarization started anywhere in the wall spreads through a large mass of muscle and many cells contract together. A coordinated squeeze generates far more useful pressure than the scattered contractions of the uncoupled organ earlier in pregnancy. Adding gap junctions pushes the tissue further toward single unit behavior, not toward multi unit independent innervation. Coupling recruits neighbors rather than wasting current, and stretch sensitivity is retained, which matters as the uterus is distended.

cards.q: Two smooth muscle preparations are studied. In preparation A, cutting the nerve supply abolishes all contraction. In preparation B, rhythmic contractions continue after the nerve is cut and a stimulus at one edge makes the whole strip contract. What are A and B?
cards.a: A is multi unit and B is single unit.
options: A is single unit and B is multi unit
A is multi unit and B is single unit
Both are single unit, differing only in innervation density
A is smooth muscle and B is cardiac muscle
cards.explanation: Preparation A depends entirely on its nerves and shows no spread of excitation, which is the signature of multi unit muscle with individually innervated, uncoupled fibers. Preparation B has intrinsic pacemaker activity and propagates excitation through gap junctions, so it is single unit. Reversing the two ignores that spontaneous rhythm and spread both require coupling. If both were single unit, cutting the nerve would not silence A. Cardiac muscle would be a fair guess from B alone, but the preparation was stated to be smooth muscle.

cards.q: Blood pressure to a resting muscle bed rises by 20 percent. Flow jumps at first, then returns nearly to its original value within a minute even though pressure stays elevated. Which combination best explains the return?
cards.a: Myogenic constriction from stretch, helped by washout of vasodilator metabolites.
options: Falling cardiac output that lowers flow back to baseline
Myogenic constriction plus washout of vasodilator metabolites
Sympathetic reflex dilation triggered by the higher pressure
A rise in blood viscosity produced by the faster flow
cards.explanation: Two local mechanisms push in the same direction here. Stretch of the arteriolar wall triggers myogenic contraction, and the initial surge in flow washes out adenosine and other dilator metabolites, so tone rises from both sides and resistance climbs until flow is close to where it started. Pressure was stated to stay elevated, so a fall in cardiac output is not the explanation. A sympathetic reflex to high pressure would reduce constrictor tone rather than dilate actively, and it is not needed since autoregulation persists in a denervated bed. Viscosity does not change appreciably over a minute.

cards.q: Which component of the intercalated disc lets current pass directly from one cardiac cell to the next?
cards.a: Gap junctions.
options: Gap junctions
The fascia adherens
Tight junctions
Desmosomes
cards.explanation: Gap junctions are pores built from connexon proteins that link the cytoplasm of neighboring myocytes, so ions carrying a depolarization flow straight into the next cell with no synapse in between. That low resistance path is what turns millions of separate cells into one conducting mass. Desmosomes and the fascia adherens are the mechanical halves of the disc: they hold cells together and transmit force. Tight junctions seal spaces between epithelial cells and are not a feature of the intercalated disc.

cards.q: Which part of the intercalated disc keeps cardiac cells from being pulled apart during a forceful contraction?
cards.a: The desmosomes and fascia adherens.
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal cisternae
The gap junctions
The T tubules at the Z line
The desmosomes and fascia adherens
cards.explanation: Desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments between cells and the fascia adherens ties the thin filaments of one cell to those of the next, so tension generated in one myocyte is handed mechanically to its neighbor. Without them the electrical connection would tear apart under load. Gap junctions handle the electrical job and are far too small to carry much force. T tubules bring the action potential into the interior of a cell, and terminal cisternae store Ca2+; neither joins cell to cell.

cards.q: Which ion current is chiefly responsible for the plateau phase of the ventricular action potential?
cards.a: Ca2+ entering through L-type Ca2+ channels.
options: K+ leaving through delayed rectifier channels
Cl- entering through anion channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type Ca2+ channels
Na+ entering through fast Na+ channels
cards.explanation: During the plateau, slow L-type Ca2+ channels stay open and the inward Ca2+ current roughly balances the outward K+ current, holding the membrane depolarized for a couple hundred milliseconds. That Ca2+ does double duty, since it also triggers Ca2+ release from the SR. Fast Na+ channels drive the upstroke and then inactivate within a few milliseconds. Delayed rectifier K+ current is present but is what finally ends the plateau when it grows, and Cl- current is not the main plateau carrier.

cards.q: About how long does a ventricular action potential last?
cards.a: Roughly 250 ms.
options: Roughly 2 ms
Roughly 25 ms
Roughly 250 ms
Roughly 2500 ms
cards.explanation: A ventricular action potential lasts on the order of 200 to 300 ms, most of it plateau, which is comparable to the duration of the contraction it produces. That match is the reason the heart cannot summate twitches. Roughly 2 ms is the skeletal muscle value, and comparing the two numbers is the fastest way to see why one tissue tetanizes and the other does not. 2500 ms would be longer than an entire cardiac cycle at rest.

cards.q: What is the absolute refractory period?
cards.a: The interval during which no stimulus, however strong, can trigger another action potential.
options: The interval when only a stronger than normal stimulus can trigger a response
The interval during which no stimulus of any strength can trigger a response
The interval when the cell is repolarized but still mechanically contracted
The interval between the action potential and the start of tension
cards.explanation: During the absolute refractory period the fast Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot be reopened at any voltage, so the cell simply will not fire again. In ventricular muscle it covers nearly the whole plateau and much of repolarization. The option about needing a stronger stimulus defines the relative refractory period that follows it, when some Na+ channels have recovered. The other choices describe mechanical timing, which is a separate matter from excitability.

cards.q: What does it mean to say the myocardium behaves as a functional syncytium?
cards.a: The cells stay separate but are so well coupled that they respond as a single unit.
options: The cells stay separate but are coupled enough to respond as one unit
The cells contract independently and their forces add up in the wall
The cells share one nerve supply that reaches every fiber directly
The cells fuse into one giant multinucleated cell during development
cards.explanation: Each myocyte keeps its own membrane and nucleus, but gap junctions couple them electrically so an impulse anywhere spreads through the whole mass and the chamber contracts all or none. That is what functional means here, as opposed to the true structural fusion seen in skeletal muscle fibers. Independent contraction is exactly what the coupling prevents, and it would make the chamber a poor pump. Cardiac cells are influenced by autonomic nerves, but the coordinated contraction does not depend on neural distribution.

cards.q: What is calcium induced calcium release in cardiac muscle?
cards.a: Ca2+ entering from outside opens ryanodine receptors and releases a larger store of Ca2+ from the SR.
options: Ca2+ leaving the SR then triggers Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane
Ca2+ binding calmodulin activates a kinase that opens the SR channels
Ca2+ pumped into the SR triggers a release of Ca2+ from mitochondria
Ca2+ entering from outside opens SR ryanodine receptors to release more
cards.explanation: A modest trigger of Ca2+ crossing the sarcolemma through L-type channels opens ryanodine receptors on the neighboring SR, and the SR supplies most of the Ca2+ that actually binds troponin. Because the trigger comes from outside, the size of the beat depends on extracellular Ca2+, unlike skeletal muscle. The reversed version has the sequence backwards. The calmodulin and kinase route is smooth muscle regulation, and mitochondria buffer Ca2+ rather than release activator Ca2+.

cards.q: What keeps the atrial syncytium electrically separate from the ventricular syncytium?
cards.a: The fibrous skeleton of the heart, which conducts only at the AV node.
options: The coronary vessels running in the AV groove
The pericardium wrapped around each chamber
The interventricular septum, which has no gap junctions
The fibrous skeleton, which conducts only at the AV node
cards.explanation: Nonconducting connective tissue rings sit between atria and ventricles, so excitation cannot cross directly and must funnel through the AV node. The delay that funnel imposes is what lets atria finish filling the ventricles before the ventricles contract. The pericardium surrounds the whole heart and plays no role in conduction. The interventricular septum is muscle and conducts well. Coronary vessels supply blood, not insulation.

cards.q: Why can skeletal muscle be tetanized while cardiac muscle cannot?
cards.a: In cardiac muscle the refractory period lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so twitches cannot summate.
options: Cardiac muscle relaxes faster than skeletal muscle, preventing summation
Cardiac muscle lacks the sarcoplasmic reticulum needed for summation
Cardiac cells are refractory almost as long as the contraction lasts
Cardiac muscle cannot be stimulated more than once per second
cards.explanation: In skeletal muscle a 2 ms action potential is long over before the twitch peaks, so a second stimulus can arrive while tension is still present and the twitches add. In cardiac muscle the long plateau keeps the cell refractory through nearly the entire contraction, so by the time another beat can be triggered the muscle has relaxed. Cardiac muscle has a working sarcoplasmic reticulum. It can be driven at three or four beats per second, just never fast enough to summate. Cardiac relaxation is slower, not faster, than skeletal.

cards.q: A drug shortens the ventricular action potential from about 250 ms to about 10 ms without changing anything else. What becomes possible, and what is the consequence for the heart?
cards.a: Twitches could summate into tetanus, and the heart could not fill.
options: Conduction between cells would stop, since gap junctions need the plateau
Twitches could summate into tetanus, and the heart could not fill
Contraction would become weaker but the rhythm would be safer
The heart would beat more slowly but pump more per beat
cards.explanation: The long refractory period exists because of the plateau, so shortening the action potential shortens the refractory period and lets a second stimulus arrive while tension is still developing. A tetanized ventricle stays contracted, never relaxes, and therefore never fills, so output falls to nothing. This is a rhythm hazard, not a safety feature. Stroke volume depends on filling, which is precisely what is lost, and gap junctions conduct current regardless of action potential shape.

cards.q: A blocker of cardiac gap junctions is applied to a sheet of ventricular myocytes, then one cell is stimulated. What is observed?
cards.a: Only that cell and its immediate neighbors contract.
options: Only that cell and its immediate neighbors contract
The whole sheet contracts, but more slowly than before
No cell contracts, since excitation requires cell to cell coupling
The whole sheet contracts as usual, since each cell is separately innervated
cards.explanation: Excitation spreads through the myocardium by current flowing through gap junctions, so blocking them isolates cells and the impulse dies out near where it started. This is why uncoupling produces slow, fragmented conduction rather than a slower whole heart beat. Cardiac muscle is not innervated fiber by fiber the way multi unit smooth muscle is. The stimulated cell itself still has intact channels and contracts normally, so a complete absence of contraction is wrong.

cards.q: A second stimulus is delivered to a ventricular myocyte 100 ms after the first, during the plateau. What happens?
cards.a: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory.
options: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory
The plateau is cut short and the cell repolarizes early
A second, smaller action potential is triggered
A full second action potential is triggered and tension adds
cards.explanation: At 100 ms the cell is still in the plateau with its fast Na+ channels inactivated, so no stimulus strength will produce another upstroke. That protection is what prevents summation of cardiac twitches. A smaller response would be possible only later, in the relative refractory period, once some Na+ channels have recovered. Tension cannot add during absolute refractoriness, and an ordinary stimulus does not truncate the plateau.

cards.q: A stimulus is delivered late in repolarization, during the relative refractory period. How does the response compare with a normal beat?
cards.a: A weaker action potential is produced, and it takes a stronger stimulus to produce it.
options: A normal action potential is produced with a stimulus of normal size
A normal action potential is produced but the tension is doubled
No response occurs at any stimulus strength at all
A weaker action potential, and only a stronger stimulus triggers it
cards.explanation: By late repolarization some fast Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation but many have not, so a larger than normal stimulus can trigger an upstroke, and that upstroke rises more slowly and conducts more slowly than usual. That premature beat is also weaker mechanically because SR Ca2+ has not fully recovered. Total unresponsiveness describes the absolute refractory period that came just before. A fully normal response requires waiting until the cell has repolarized completely.

cards.q: Since cardiac muscle can neither recruit more fibers nor summate twitches, how does the heart increase the force of a beat?
cards.a: By raising the Ca2+ available per beat and by stretching the fibers before contraction.
options: By shortening the refractory period so more cross bridges can attach
By recruiting the reserve myocytes that stayed silent on the previous beat
By raising Ca2+ per beat and by stretching the fibers before contraction
By firing action potentials at a higher frequency until twitches fuse
cards.explanation: Every beat already activates every cell, so the two available levers are how much Ca2+ reaches troponin, which sympathetic stimulation increases, and how much the fibers are stretched by filling, which is the length tension relationship. There is no reserve pool of silent myocytes to recruit; that idea belongs to motor unit recruitment in skeletal muscle. Fusion of twitches is exactly what refractoriness prevents. A shorter refractory period would threaten rhythm without adding cross bridges to a single beat.

cards.q: An L-type Ca2+ channel blocker is applied to a ventricular myocyte. Predict the effect on the strength of contraction and give the reason.
cards.a: Contraction weakens, because less trigger Ca2+ enters and the SR releases less.
options: Contraction is unchanged, because troponin is already saturated with Ca2+
Contraction weakens, because less trigger Ca2+ enters and the SR releases less
Contraction strengthens, because Ca2+ stays in the SR for the next beat
Contraction is unchanged, because activator Ca2+ is entirely SR derived
cards.explanation: Cardiac contraction depends on calcium induced calcium release, so the amount of Ca2+ crossing the sarcolemma sets how much the SR adds, and blocking the L-type channel scales the whole beat down. The same drug barely changes skeletal muscle force, which is the comparison worth remembering. Retaining Ca2+ in the SR does not help if there is no trigger to release it. Troponin is far from saturated during a normal beat, which is why beat strength can be graded at all.

cards.q: In a region of ischemic myocardium, connexons close and the cells uncouple electrically. Trace the consequences for conduction through that region and for the pumping of the chamber.
cards.a: Conduction slows or fails through the region, and the chamber contracts unevenly and pumps less.
options: Conduction speeds up locally, and the chamber contracts more forcefully
Conduction slows or fails there, and the chamber contracts unevenly and pumps less
Conduction is unaffected, since impulses travel through the interstitial fluid
Conduction stops everywhere in the heart, since one syncytium is lost
cards.explanation: Current spreading from cell to cell needs open gap junctions, so uncoupling raises the resistance of the path and the impulse crawls or blocks. Muscle that is excited late, or not at all, contracts out of step with the rest of the wall, so some regions are still shortening while others are already relaxing and less pressure is developed. Uncoupling can never speed conduction. Impulses do not travel usefully through interstitial fluid between cells. The rest of the syncytium remains coupled, so the whole heart does not stop.

cards.q: A ventricular strip is stimulated, then a test stimulus is applied at varying delays. At 150 ms there is no response at any strength; at 250 ms a strong stimulus gives a small beat; at 400 ms a normal stimulus gives a full beat. What do these results show?
cards.a: The absolute refractory period ends between 150 and 250 ms, and full recovery takes about 400 ms.
options: Absolute refractoriness ends between 150 and 250 ms, full recovery near 400 ms
The muscle was fatigued at 150 ms and had recovered its ATP by 400 ms
The tissue was briefly tetanized at 250 ms, producing that small extra beat
The action potential lasts only 150 ms, since a response appeared after that
cards.explanation: Failure at any strength marks absolute refractoriness, a response only to a strong stimulus marks the relative refractory period, and a normal response to a normal stimulus means the cell has fully recovered. Reading the three delays in order gives the timing of recovery directly. The 150 ms result puts a lower bound on refractoriness, not the exact action potential duration. Fatigue would not resolve on this timescale and would not depend on stimulus strength. A single small beat is a premature response, not tetanus.

cards.q: A drug lengthens the ventricular action potential by 100 ms. Predict its effects on the refractory period and on the highest heart rate the ventricle can follow.
cards.a: The refractory period lengthens and the maximum rate the ventricle can follow falls.
options: The refractory period lengthens but maximum rate is set by the SA node alone
The refractory period shortens, since repolarization is spread over more time
Neither changes, because refractoriness depends only on Na+ channel number
The refractory period lengthens and the maximum followable rate falls
cards.explanation: The refractory period is tied to the action potential, since Na+ channels recover from inactivation only as the membrane repolarizes, so a longer plateau means a longer wait before the next beat is possible. If beats cannot be triggered more often than about once per refractory period, the ceiling on ventricular rate drops. The SA node sets the rate it tries to impose, but the ventricle can only follow what its own refractoriness allows. A longer action potential cannot shorten refractoriness, and refractory timing depends on the voltage course, not on channel number alone.

cards.q: Two muscle preparations are stimulated at 50 Hz. Preparation X fuses into a smooth sustained contraction; preparation Y produces separate beats at the same rate the stimulator allows and never fuses. Which is cardiac, and what single property explains the difference?
cards.a: Y is cardiac, because its refractory period covers nearly the whole contraction.
options: X is cardiac, because only cardiac muscle can maintain sustained tension
X is cardiac, because its cells are electrically coupled and contract together
Y is cardiac, because its refractory period covers nearly the whole contraction
Y is cardiac, because it lacks a sarcoplasmic reticulum to sustain Ca2+
cards.explanation: Fusion requires that a second stimulus arrive while tension from the first is still present, and cardiac muscle stays refractory for nearly the entire twitch, so it simply cannot be restimulated in that window. Preparation X, which fuses, must be skeletal. Electrical coupling explains why cardiac cells beat together, but coupling has nothing to do with whether twitches summate. Cardiac muscle does have a sarcoplasmic reticulum. Sustained tetanic tension is a skeletal capability, and for a pump it would be a disaster, since a ventricle that never relaxes never fills.

cards.q: In which muscle types does Ca2+ start contraction by binding troponin C on the thin filament?
cards.a: Skeletal and cardiac muscle.
options: All three muscle types
Skeletal muscle only
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated and both use the troponin tropomyosin complex, so Ca2+ binding troponin C swings tropomyosin off the myosin binding sites. Smooth muscle has no troponin at all, which is why it cannot be on this list, and it is the single most useful fact for telling the three tissues apart mechanistically. Answering skeletal only forgets that cardiac thin filaments carry the same regulatory proteins. Grouping cardiac with smooth mixes a thin filament system with a thick filament one.

cards.q: In which muscle type is the Ca2+ binding regulatory protein a soluble cytosolic protein rather than part of the thin filament?
cards.a: Smooth muscle.
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac and skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle uses calmodulin, which floats free in the cytosol and, once it has bound Ca2+, activates myosin light chain kinase. Because the switch ends up on the myosin head, smooth muscle regulation is called thick filament regulation. Skeletal and cardiac muscle both attach the Ca2+ sensor to the thin filament as troponin C, so the switch sits on actin rather than on myosin. That difference in where the switch lives predicts almost everything else about the three tissues.

cards.q: How much of the activator Ca2+ for a skeletal muscle twitch comes from outside the cell?
cards.a: Essentially none; the sarcoplasmic reticulum supplies it.
options: Essentially none of it
None during a twitch, but all during tetanus
Essentially all of it
About half of it
cards.explanation: In skeletal muscle the voltage sensor in the T tubule membrane opens the SR release channel by direct mechanical coupling, so no Ca2+ needs to cross the plasma membrane for a twitch to occur. That self sufficiency is why a skeletal fiber keeps twitching in a Ca2+ free bath and why Ca2+ channel blockers do not weaken it. Cardiac and smooth muscle are the tissues that depend on Ca2+ entry. Tetanus is repeated activation of the same mechanism, so the Ca2+ source does not change.

cards.q: Which muscle types require Ca2+ to cross the plasma membrane for each contraction?
cards.a: Cardiac and smooth muscle.
options: Skeletal and smooth muscle
All three types equally
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Cardiac muscle needs a trigger of entering Ca2+ to open ryanodine receptors, and smooth muscle relies on entering Ca2+ for most of its activator supply, so both tissues are sensitive to extracellular Ca2+ and to Ca2+ channel blockers. Skeletal muscle is the exception, since its T tubule voltage sensor opens the SR channel mechanically. Any option that includes skeletal muscle in the entry dependent group misses that mechanical coupling. The three are not equal here, and this is exactly the difference that experiments in low Ca2+ solutions expose.

cards.q: In which muscle type does the Ca2+ regulated switch sit on the myosin head rather than on actin?
cards.a: Smooth muscle.
options: Skeletal muscle
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
cards.explanation: In smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates a regulatory light chain on the myosin head, so the thick filament carries the on switch. In skeletal and cardiac muscle the switch is on the thin filament, where troponin and tropomyosin control access to the myosin binding sites. Because a kinase has to act before a smooth muscle cross bridge can cycle, contraction there begins more slowly than in either striated tissue. Recognizing which filament holds the switch tells you which drugs and which second messengers can change tension.

cards.q: Which muscle type grades the force of contraction by recruiting more motor units?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle.
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Only skeletal muscle is organized into motor units, each a somatic motor neuron and the fibers it controls, so the nervous system can add units to add force. Cardiac muscle is a syncytium and activates every cell on every beat, leaving nothing to recruit, so it grades force through Ca2+ per beat and fiber length instead. Smooth muscle grades force through the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated. Recruitment requires separate control of separate fibers, which the coupled tissues do not have.

cards.q: Which muscle type takes the longest to reach peak tension and can hold that tension the longest?
cards.a: Smooth muscle.
options: Slow twitch skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Fast twitch skeletal muscle
cards.explanation: Smooth muscle can take a second or more to reach peak tension, because a kinase must phosphorylate myosin and the myosin ATPase is very slow, and the same slow cycling lets it hold tension for hours at low ATP cost. Cardiac muscle contracts in a couple hundred milliseconds and must relax to allow filling, so long holding is not an option. Fast twitch skeletal fibers peak in tens of milliseconds and fatigue quickly. Slow twitch fibers are more fatigue resistant than fast ones but are still far faster and more expensive than smooth muscle.

cards.q: Which muscle types can generate their own rhythmic excitation without any input from a nerve?
cards.a: Cardiac muscle and single unit smooth muscle.
options: Cardiac and single unit smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle
Multi unit smooth muscle only
Skeletal muscle alone
cards.explanation: Pacemaker activity requires cells with unstable resting potentials plus gap junctions to spread the rhythm, and both the heart and single unit smooth muscle have them, which is why a denervated heart still beats and an isolated loop of intestine still shows waves. Skeletal muscle is quiet without its motor neuron, so any option containing it is wrong. Multi unit smooth muscle is largely uncoupled and depends on its nerves, which is what makes its control precise rather than rhythmic.

cards.q: A cardiac myocyte and a skeletal fiber are moved into a Ca2+ free solution and stimulated. Which stops contracting first, and why?
cards.a: The cardiac myocyte, because it needs entering Ca2+ to trigger SR release.
options: The cardiac myocyte, because it needs entering Ca2+ to trigger SR release
They stop together, since both depend on the same SR store of Ca2+
Neither stops, since both release all of their Ca2+ from the SR
The skeletal fiber, because it holds a smaller store of Ca2+ in its SR
cards.explanation: Cardiac contraction depends on calcium induced calcium release, so within a few beats there is no trigger Ca2+ and the SR stops releasing, even though the store itself is still there. Skeletal muscle opens its SR channel mechanically from the T tubule voltage sensor, so it keeps twitching until the store runs down. The skeletal SR is the larger, better loaded store, not the smaller one. The two tissues do not behave alike here, and this experiment is the cleanest demonstration of that difference in Ca2+ source.

cards.q: A drug binds troponin C and prevents Ca2+ from binding it. Which tissues lose the ability to contract?
cards.a: Skeletal and cardiac muscle, with smooth muscle unaffected.
options: Cardiac and smooth muscle, with skeletal muscle unaffected
All three muscle types
Smooth muscle only
Skeletal and cardiac muscle, with smooth muscle unaffected
cards.explanation: The drug can only work where its target exists, and troponin is a thin filament protein of striated muscle. Smooth muscle has no troponin and routes Ca2+ through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase instead, so it goes on contracting. Saying all three assumes a shared mechanism that the tissues do not share. The options that spare skeletal muscle or hit smooth muscle alone reverse which tissues carry troponin, which is the fact this card is asking you to reason from.

cards.q: A drug inhibits calmodulin. Which muscle tissue loses the ability to contract, and why?
cards.a: Smooth muscle, because Ca2+ reaches myosin only through calmodulin there.
options: Cardiac muscle, because calmodulin triggers Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release
All three, because calmodulin is the universal Ca2+ sensor
Smooth muscle, because Ca2+ reaches myosin only through calmodulin there
Skeletal muscle, because calmodulin activates its SR release channel
cards.explanation: In smooth muscle, Ca2+ has no direct effect on the contractile machinery; it must bind calmodulin, and Ca2+ calmodulin must activate myosin light chain kinase. Remove calmodulin from that chain and a normal Ca2+ signal produces no tension. Skeletal and cardiac muscle route Ca2+ through troponin C, so their twitch is intact. Calmodulin is present in nearly all cells and does many jobs, but it is not the trigger for striated muscle contraction, so it is not universal in that sense.

cards.q: A patient takes a Ca2+ channel blocker that relaxes arteries and reduces the force of cardiac contraction. Why is skeletal muscle strength essentially unchanged?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle does not need Ca2+ entry, since its SR release is triggered mechanically.
options: Skeletal muscle uses a different regulatory protein, so channel blockers cannot bind
Skeletal muscle does not need Ca2+ entry, since its SR release is triggered mechanically
Skeletal muscle contracts too quickly for the drug to take effect
Skeletal muscle receives less blood flow, so the drug concentration is lower
cards.explanation: The drug lowers Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane, and only tissues that depend on entry feel it. In skeletal muscle the T tubule voltage sensor opens the SR release channel by physical coupling, so entering Ca2+ is not part of the pathway and force is preserved. The regulatory protein difference is real but is not what saves skeletal muscle here, since the drug acts on channels rather than on troponin. Speed of contraction and blood flow do not determine whether a pathway needs Ca2+ entry.

cards.q: An unlabeled muscle strip develops peak tension slowly over about a second and then holds that tension for many minutes at very low ATP cost. From that behavior alone, which regulatory system is it most likely using?
cards.a: Calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase acting on the myosin head.
options: Troponin and tropomyosin on the thin filament, with a fast myosin ATPase
Calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase acting on the myosin head
Troponin regulation combined with a long plateau action potential
Direct Ca2+ binding to myosin with no regulatory protein involved
cards.explanation: Slow onset points to an enzymatic step between the Ca2+ signal and the cross bridge, and cheap maintained tension points to slowly cycling latch bridges, and both are hallmarks of the calmodulin and MLCK system with its slow myosin. Troponin regulation with a fast ATPase would give a twitch in tens of milliseconds and would cost far more ATP to hold. Troponin plus a long plateau describes cardiac muscle, which contracts in a few hundred milliseconds and must relax to refill. No vertebrate muscle activates by Ca2+ binding myosin without a regulatory protein.

cards.q: A single stimulus produces an all or none twitch in a skeletal fiber, but graded tension in a smooth muscle cell. What accounts for the graded response in smooth muscle?
cards.a: Tension tracks the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated.
options: Tension tracks the fraction of myosin light chains that are phosphorylated
Smooth muscle recruits more cells as the stimulus grows stronger
Smooth muscle action potentials vary in amplitude with stimulus strength
Only some sarcomeres in the smooth muscle cell are activated at a time
cards.explanation: The amount of Ca2+ in a smooth muscle cell sets how much MLCK activity there is, that sets what fraction of myosin heads carry a phosphate, and tension follows that fraction, so intermediate levels of activation give intermediate tension. In a skeletal fiber a single action potential dumps enough SR Ca2+ to saturate troponin, so the twitch is all or none. Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres to activate selectively. Recruiting more cells grades the tissue response but not the response of one cell, and action potentials are all or none wherever they occur.

cards.q: Cytosolic Ca2+ falls at a similar rate in a smooth muscle cell and a skeletal fiber after stimulation, yet the smooth muscle stays contracted much longer. Why?
cards.a: A phosphatase must remove phosphate from each myosin light chain before those bridges stop cycling.
options: Smooth muscle has no mechanism at all for pumping Ca2+ back out
Smooth muscle myosin binds actin irreversibly once tension develops
Smooth muscle Ca2+ stays bound to troponin after cytosolic Ca2+ falls
A phosphatase must strip phosphate from each myosin light chain first
cards.explanation: In skeletal muscle, relaxation follows Ca2+ removal almost immediately because Ca2+ simply leaves troponin. In smooth muscle the Ca2+ signal has already been converted into phosphorylated myosin, and that phosphate has to be removed by myosin light chain phosphatase before the heads stop cycling, which adds a further delay. Troponin is not present in smooth muscle. Smooth muscle does have Ca2+ pumps in the SR and the plasma membrane. Attachment is reversible, or the muscle could never relax at all.

cards.q: An unlabeled tissue contracts when it is stretched, shows no striations, holds tension for long periods with little ATP use, and is completely unaffected by a drug that blocks Ca2+ binding to troponin. Which tissue is it, and which two facts identify it?
cards.a: Smooth muscle, identified by calmodulin regulation and the slow, economical cross bridge cycle.
options: Cardiac muscle, identified by its long plateau and its syncytial coupling
Slow twitch skeletal muscle, identified by fatigue resistance and troponin
Smooth muscle, identified by calmodulin regulation and slow economical cycling
Multi unit smooth muscle, identified by the absence of any Ca2+ requirement
cards.explanation: Insensitivity to a troponin drug rules out both striated tissues at once, since only smooth muscle regulates through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase. Long cheap tension is the latch behavior that follows from the very slow smooth muscle myosin ATPase, and stretch induced contraction is the myogenic response. Cardiac muscle would have been silenced by the troponin drug and cannot hold tension without failing as a pump. Slow twitch skeletal fibers still use troponin. Smooth muscle certainly requires Ca2+; it simply routes it differently.

cards.q: An unlabeled tissue has action potentials lasting about 250 ms, cannot be tetanized, loses much of its force when extracellular Ca2+ is halved, and is silenced by a drug that blocks Ca2+ binding to troponin. Which tissue is it, and which two findings separate it from skeletal muscle?
cards.a: Cardiac muscle, separated by its dependence on entering Ca2+ and by its long refractory period.
options: Cardiac muscle, separated by its use of calmodulin rather than troponin
Smooth muscle, separated by its slow contraction and its calmodulin based regulation
Cardiac muscle, separated by dependence on entering Ca2+ and a long refractory period
Skeletal muscle, separated only by the presence of gap junctions between cells
cards.explanation: The troponin drug works, so the tissue is striated, which leaves skeletal or cardiac. Two findings then point to cardiac: force falls when extracellular Ca2+ drops, which fits calcium induced calcium release rather than the self sufficient skeletal SR, and the long action potential makes the refractory period cover the contraction so tetanus is impossible. Smooth muscle is excluded by its sensitivity to the troponin drug. Calling it cardiac because of calmodulin contradicts the same finding, since cardiac muscle regulates through troponin.

cards.q: A toxin blocks ryanodine receptors. Predict its effect on a skeletal fiber and on a smooth muscle cell, and explain the difference.
cards.a: The skeletal twitch is nearly abolished while smooth muscle still contracts, because smooth muscle gets most of its Ca2+ from outside and through IP3 receptors.
options: Both are abolished, since both tissues release all activator Ca2+ through ryanodine receptors
The skeletal twitch is nearly abolished while smooth muscle contracts on, using entering Ca2+ and IP3 receptors
Smooth muscle contraction is abolished while skeletal muscle is unaffected, since only smooth muscle has an SR
Neither tissue is affected, since ryanodine receptors are found only in cardiac muscle cells
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle sends essentially all of its activator Ca2+ through the ryanodine receptor, opened mechanically by the T tubule voltage sensor, so blocking that channel takes the twitch away. Smooth muscle draws most of its Ca2+ across the plasma membrane and releases the rest through IP3 receptors, so it has routes the toxin does not touch. Skeletal muscle has by far the more developed SR, so the third option has the tissues backwards. Ryanodine receptors are present in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle, not in the heart alone.

cards.q: Two strips reach the same peak tension. Strip 1 gets there in about 50 ms and burns ATP rapidly; strip 2 takes about 1.5 s and then holds tension with very little further ATP use. Explain the difference in terms of the regulatory protein and the myosin.
cards.a: Strip 1 uses troponin with a fast myosin ATPase; strip 2 phosphorylates myosin through MLCK and cycles slowly.
options: Strip 1 uses troponin with a fast myosin ATPase, while strip 2 uses MLCK and cycles slowly
Strip 1 stores more Ca2+, so it can afford to spend ATP faster
Strip 2 has a longer action potential, which spreads the same ATP cost over more time
Strip 2 simply has more cross bridges, so each one works less hard
cards.explanation: Speed of onset is set by how directly the Ca2+ signal reaches the cross bridge, and Ca2+ binding troponin is immediate while an MLCK phosphorylation step is not. ATP cost per unit tension is set by cycling rate, and the slow smooth muscle myosin, with latch bridges that hang on after dephosphorylation, holds force for a fraction of the ATP. More cross bridges would not reduce the ATP each cycle costs. Ca2+ storage does not change the price of a cross bridge cycle, and action potential duration does not set the rate of ATP hydrolysis by myosin.
